headline: Bunker Tighten in Oyster Creek — First Fall Stripers Show, Blues Still Thick at the Inlet
subhead: Forty years of watching the September mullet run tells you the same thing every time: when the peanuts bunch up in the back creeks, the stripers aren't far behind.
body_markdown:
There's a September I remember from the early '90s when the mullet run came through so thick off Good Luck Point that the water looked like it was boiling from underneath — not bait scattering, but bait balling up so tight the surface just trembled. My old mate on the Point Pleasant boats, a Portuguese fella named Manny, used to say you could smell that run before you saw it, something sweet and muddy on the wind out of the marsh. That's the smell that's been drifting off Double Creek and Oyster Creek this week, and it means the same thing it always has — the bay's flipping over into fall.

The full moon that came through the 6th and 7th did exactly what we said it would do a few days back — tightened the bunker schools up hard. Anybody running Oyster Creek or the flats south of Good Luck Point this week saw it: peanut bunker packed into balls the size of a rowboat, nervous water everywhere, and now the first real striper interest showing instead of just a stray fish picking at the edges. We flagged this — said the peanut density building inside the bay would trigger the first real activity once a cool front knocked the water down a few degrees, and that's the stage we're on now. The front hasn't fully arrived yet, but the moon did the tightening for us, and the bass are starting to lean in.

Don't expect blitz conditions yet — this is early. What's happening is scattered but real: schoolie bass and the occasional slot fish working the bunker pods on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, mostly at dawn and again at dusk, in the deeper cuts along Double Creek Channel and the mouth of Oyster Creek where the warm water discharge still holds a slight edge in temperature. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Ava jigs in white — worked through the edges of the bait balls has been the better call than trying to match the peanuts exactly. If you can find bass actually busting on top, which has happened sporadically around Tices Shoal on the last of the ebb, a topwater like a Yo-Zuri popper will get bit, but most of the fish right now are working underneath the bait, not on it.

Bluefish have not slowed down one bit and honestly they're the more dependable bite through the middle of the day right now. Blues to three and four pounds are chopping through the same bunker schools in Barnegat Inlet on the incoming, and out along the Island Beach surf where the bunker pods push tight to the beach on a rising tide. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, or just a bare bucktail bounced through the melee, gets hit fast. If you're marking bunker on the sounder anywhere between the Coast Guard station and the north jetty, there are blues under it — that part of the pattern hasn't changed all summer.

Fluke are winding down the way they always do this time of year, but there's still a decent tail end of the season for anyone willing to work the channel edges. Double Creek Channel is still producing keepers to five pounds on the last of the incoming tide, drifting 4-inch white Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the deeper bends where the current stacks bait against the drop-off. The bite has gotten shorter — an hour and a half around the tide change instead of the all-day grazing you get in July — so timing matters more than it did a month ago. Expect this fishery to keep tapering through the rest of September as those fish start staging for their run out the inlet.

Kingfish are still around the sod banks and sandy pockets inside Barnegat Inlet and along the edges of Tices Shoal, though the bite has thinned from its August peak. Bloodworms or Fishbites on a high-low rig in three to six feet of moving water, fished right on bottom, will still put a few in the bucket for anyone patient enough to sit on it through a tide. Blowfish are hanging in similar water — the docks and bulkheads around Forked River and up into Toms River creeks still have them stacked up on clam snapper rigs, a fun target for kids and a reliable one when the bigger stuff is being stubborn.

Weakfish have been the quiet story of early September. The mullet run pushing through the back marshes near the sedges south of Double Creek has pulled a few marsh-run weakfish up shallow on the last two hours of the falling tide, taking small white paddletails worked slow along the grass edges. It's not the May sedge bite by any stretch, but it's worth a look for anyone working that stretch at last light.

Looking at the next several days, the pattern to watch is straightforward: as nights keep cooling into mid-September and that first real cold front finally pushes through, expect the bunker density we're seeing now in Oyster Creek and Double Creek to tip over into the first legitimate bay blitz of the fall. It won't happen on a calendar — it'll happen the first morning the water temp drops two or three degrees overnight and the bass decide the bait's worth committing to instead of just shadowing. Until then, work the tide changes around the bunker schools, keep the metal light and fast, and don't be surprised if the better fish this week come from anglers who put in time on bluefish instead of waiting on stripers that aren't fully switched on yet.
